Props to the dev as there's some interesting ideas, and it just entered Early Access so stuff is likely to change, but currently I just don't find it fun. The world seems interesting and I like the idea of "rebuilding" the hub area. Unfortunately I don't find the combat to be great. The main character is pretty floaty, and your attacks don't seem to stun enemies like you think they should, leading to a lot of cheap hits - and since there's usually a crowd, that damage adds up. I stuck with a melee build, maybe magic would have done better, but most of the equipment I found either wasn't very useful or had some serious drawbacks. And I didn't see the point of the Hope/Despair system. The first couple of levels I was dipping into Despair, but after that my Hope was always pretty high. I got to level eight of the first area, then died due to several rooms with crowds of mobs. I thought I must be missing something, so I checked the reviews and discussions. When I learned that only a few builds are currently viable, and that you need to grind for Hopestones and materials to upgrade your gear, that cemented my decision to refund. Again, Early Access, but I can't recommend it right now.

The game starts out strong with level variety, a great atmosphere and interesting mechanics. However very soon you realize there is not that much content yet. I realize this is an early acces game but under three hours you will run into messages saying that areas are still under development. As somebody else pointed out, there is a demo but the full game does not have that much more. There is loads of potential but I cannot recommend it at the current state. Especially not for the current price tag which is frankly ridiculous for the amount of content. I also find the positive comments extremely misleading in regards to the item combinations and "interesting builds". If I were a more paranoid man I would say they were put there on purpose to get you to buy this game. A quote from the developer about the game being in early access: “The game currently has the first of 5 zones built out, plus an end game area where you can attempt runs of increasing difficulty." Seeing as I ran into "Under development messages" before reaching the end of the first zone this is simply not true. I wish the developer best of luck with their ambitions. There is definitely potential here but it's not there yet by a long shot.

Its a cool concept but if this game finds sucsess it will have to basically be rebuilt in terms of gameplay. Also the brightness is way too low. For anyone not gaming in a basement (i game on the go) it is almost impossible to see the game. You can turn it up a little from within the game. Also the crt filter looks bad just turn it off. There is no reason a game designed not on a CRT for a real crt should be used with that filter. Likely this game will be abandoned by the dev imo. If not great.

I wish there was a middle ground here. I like the exploration, all the stuff you have to unlock, the systems are cool, but like oh man the combat can be rough. Some of these encounters are incomprehensible and I have no idea what I should be doing. Like if I get trapped in a small room with 50 enemies, there's not really all that much you can do to kite or crowd control unless your build is directly made for it. Enemies either spam projectiles or have a massive lunge with little indication about their attack unless you memorize the timing (and they lunge with a follow-up attack), and they are always staggered from eachother so you can dodge a couple of them but then there are others ready to attack you when you've already dodged. And there's definitely some builds where I have no idea how you would play them. Like if I wanted to play an archer, if you can kite its generally fine but most ranged weapons dont really stun and generally done pierce so if youre in a small room with a crowd I'm not sure what you're supposed to do. The meta really feels like "stun the crowd with CC" and if you cant do that you're going to run into rooms that are just designed to kill you. And because of the lunge mechanic on mobs, melee weapons feel terrible without the unique that lets you dash while attacking. In general many of the fights feel incomprehensible. There's too many things going on at once, and its hard to even recognize what i'm being hit by or sometimes even when i'm getting hit. Not sure how it will be addressed or if it will at all (im sure people would love to comment "skill issue" here). Maybe not every single enemy needs to be designed with lunge attacks. I'll reinstall in a bit when the game has had more time to cook cause I think this has the bones of a great game.

本来总体还是好评，但是第三章开始的地形掉希望让我非常不爽，加上之前零零散散的一些槽点就一起给个差评吧。当然这游戏优点很多我就不赘述了，这篇主要说缺点 首先如果作者想推加希望的好感和相关药剂装备，我觉得大可把希望上限提高，单位兑换量减少，而不是现在这样地形本来就减速还扣希望负反馈拉满，而且这才图3，我不知道后面会怎么恶心人。 其次就是一些前面的小问题，例如没地图，本来我是无所谓的，没地图顶多多花点时间跑图，也不是没玩过这种游戏，但是到了图3地形扣希望的情况下还要满地图找漏下的怪和出口，这真的有意思吗？这就是作者希望的游戏体验吗，如果是我没什么好说的差评不冤。然后就是关卡设计问题，关卡内容不明写在标题上，需要你一个一个去试探其中内容，你当然可以说这是保持探索感，但是这游戏换个大关关卡名全部变了你前面记得全部白记真的有点脱裤放屁的感觉。最后是第一个boss骷髅王，非要设计拖时间的3段锁血，而且三段锁血还要重新跑三次图，玩了20年游戏这么烂的设计都不多见。 最后说一下这游戏的刷子部分，融合装备是很好的点，但是这游戏并没有随机数值，导致其实每个部件只需要刷一件就行了，这当然是见仁见智的机制，我个人不太喜欢因为游戏寿命会显著缩短。作为刷子游戏本身背包没办法扩充也有点偏小，然后也没有装备筛选和整理功能，非常影响体验。以上

As Early Access evolved I saw my fun in this game getting thinner and thinner. My build got nerfed and cancelled several times overnight, you can no longer reduce Despair meter from hub, and there is this weird roadmap focus on endgame chadlords for some reason, because 2024 I guess. Necrovale went from a clumsy yet amusing dungeon crawling sandbox, to a meta-based dark-souls roguelike. Though if you are to start the game from now, it should be "interesting" enough. Fun ? I let you be judge with this new version. Just don't be too attached to your build as it may very well become garbage after some "minor" changes. The game has great atmosphere though, 2D art is dope, animations are fine. There also is a lot of experimenting available considering the huge amount of items. But maybe that's for the worst, because it's an everbalancing mess to adress, and the game will let you know what is relevant to play or not eventually cutting all your hopes to play as you really wish. Anyway, the dungeons and bestiary are pretty cool and varied. The NPC encounter system is entertaining enough and makes sure you grind a little in order to fulfill quests or upgrade characters for better trade-offs. In the end, Necroval has big potential and despite my many concerns about the dev choices, he is always answering and hard at work. So, kudo to this mindset. I am mostly sour because I thought I could keep on playing this game with my favorite build through updates. Restarting from zero is always an option, but I just don't want to in current circumstances. I invested 35hrs in this game, and to be fair I loved it probably 30hrs overall. The last 5 hours were just me trying to polish my beloved build and make way through the new balancing, to no avail it seems. And I am too frustrated to give it another go with so many items I don't care about anymore. Who knows, I may come back in years, after more balancing and new features, for a fresh new start then. But for now it feels no more like the game I purchased. I just hope it meets its playerbase and get successful enough to make it up for my next dive.

Just overdamage everything with a bit of poise - no need of evade, health or defense at all - sequence stat - more than 6 (I risked to had 32 in total to check how much slideshow it will be) - slows down game speed drastically, character barely moves on the screen. reported. - no defense from poison puddles, they can instakill on increased difficulty - no further meta progression currently, after X enhancement and triple-melt there is nothing to do - expected bit more variety of orange (legendary) equipment, some types are just garbage (body, helms).

I'll give it a thumbs up, purely since the rogue like mode exists. Music and graphics are good too. The tutorial isn't good, I didn't realize I had a dodge roll until i got an item that told me it existed. The balance is pretty interesting. Since some items are objectively better than others, and you can repeat levels. Once the Merchant's quest line is finished, you can equip the item to repeat easy levels to get really good items and that is without considering drop rarity items you could get. The levels themselves are very repetitive where you can see the same map with the same enemies 10 times in the first area alone. So it really only exists so you can grind for bosses to get a good build to instakill them. I would play the other areas, but seeing how you don't auto unlock them, and have to get a certain amount of hope to spend to open it is dumb. At least offer a discount when beating the previous area, since everything but 1 costing around 100 with only getting 8 hope in the later levels of the first dungeon really forces the player to only choose one option. But like other stuff I wish it was told beforehand. But either way I don't really have a drive to deal with it, since it's going to be the same boring levels repeated too much. Once you get a good build, enemies and bosses can be shredded in seconds. The Rogue like mode fixes most of the gameplay problems right away with preventing grind and heavily limiting compared, to the main game, how many areas you get to access. I was able to actually fight some of the bosses without one-shotting them. If the Rogue Like mode didn't exist and I didn't get it for free, I would have refunded. But 100% worth it for the rogue like mode as it's much more fun and better paced. I hope the dev realizes this on their next game to get set pace like it.

1.背包与物品箱小得可怜 2.还无检索、分类、一键整理、排序功能（十二个槽位要自己一个个去看物品简介） 3.地图太暗了导致很费眼睛 4.玩法主要是装备合成，结果刚开始还只有两个槽位的装备可以合，升一级加两个槽位 玩起来是还行的，但以上四点至少要改两点才值得我给出好评。 1.The backpack and inventory are ridiculously small. 2.There is also a lack of search, sorting, one-click organization, and categorization functions (you have to manually check the description of each item to fit the twelve slots). 3.The map is too dark, making it hard on the eyes. 4.The main gameplay revolves around equipment synthesis, but at the beginning, you can only synthesize equipment in two slots, and you gain two more slots per level up. The gameplay is decent, but at least two of the above four issues need to be addressed for me to give it a positive review.

Game is fun and provides an interesting take on the genre. Being able to combine items into really interesting interactions can be lots of fun. However, the core mechanic of the game is called despair, and if you die with 100 of it (full meter) you are forced to lose an item from your equipped pieces. It's just gone and you have to farm and try to get it back. The problem is that losing the item can be such a devastating blow to a build that you'll be required to farm levels you've already completed (and probably farmed over and over already). This isn't a fun mechanic. It just feels bad. There's no joy. It makes you walk into the room and watch over and over as you struggle to pay to get it to pick the ONE item you think you miiiiiight be ok without. It's a roguelite dungeon crawler, so I expect to die and try over and over to get stronger, but losing items and having to create a new build is not fun. Ultimately I've chosen to play other games in the genre without this mechanic that are just as rewarding and engaging.

This game is a mind-numbing, grueling loop of two-three types of rooms filled with one-dimensional goblins or skeletons; that repetition is framing one really unsatisfying progression system. No matter how they call these identical dungeons, they're just filler for the monotone grind. No matter how many crystals I receive, I'm always a few short like it's a mobile game. No matter how much I invest into that stupid merchant, his stock is always a nothing burger. I've been playing for hours and I still haven't found anything better than some pea-shooter which was my very first drop. Not because it's good, because itemization here is just bad for some reason. This game is dull, stingy, and simultaneously too easy. I think the closest thing to such an insipid aftertaste I had after wasting my time on Hero Siege. Another idiotic grindfest with no elegance to it, yet even Hero Siege had the decency to last for a while. I usually can stand such tedium when the flow is right, but Necrovale ran dry for me in record terms. Based on appearances, I expected some crunch, but everything about it is kinda mushy in practice. I think I figured out a precise analogy for such games. It's like chewing on tar, which isn't as bad as it sounds, but also hardly better than nothing.

Into the Necrovale is a dark fantasy action RPG that thrives on mystery, experimentation, and rewarding player-driven progression. Developed by CLYDE games and published by Poysky Productions and Tribal-Storm, the game transports players into a cursed land known as the Necrovale, a place where criminals, exiles, and forgotten souls have been cast aside for generations. Rather than relying on lengthy storytelling sequences, the game builds its world through exploration, atmosphere, and the gradual discovery of its secrets. This approach creates an experience that feels immersive and intriguing from the very beginning. Players assume the role of The Stranger, a condemned individual sent into a realm filled with danger and uncertainty. The setting immediately establishes a bleak tone, presenting a world shaped by suffering, ruin, and ancient mysteries. Every region explored feels like a fragment of a larger history waiting to be uncovered. The game does not reveal all its answers at once, encouraging players to investigate the environment, meet unusual characters, and piece together the truth behind the Necrovale and its many inhabitants. Combat serves as the foundation of the experience and strikes an effective balance between accessibility and depth. Battles are fast, responsive, and often demanding, especially when facing larger groups of enemies or powerful bosses. Success is not determined solely by reflexes but also by understanding how different equipment pieces interact with one another. Players who enjoy experimenting with character builds will find plenty to appreciate, as the game constantly encourages creative approaches to combat. The loot system is undoubtedly the centerpiece of Into the Necrovale. The game offers an enormous collection of equipment, including weapons, armor, magical artifacts, jewelry, books, shields, staffs, and numerous other items. What makes these items special is that they do far more than simply increase statistics. Many possess unique properties that can dramatically alter combat performance when combined with other gear. Discovering unexpected synergies becomes one of the most satisfying aspects of the adventure, transforming even ordinary loot drops into exciting opportunities. This emphasis on item interaction creates a strong sense of experimentation throughout the game. Instead of chasing a single optimal build, players are encouraged to adapt and discover combinations that suit their preferred playstyle. One playthrough may focus on overwhelming damage output, while another may revolve around survivability, status effects, or unconventional strategies. Because of this flexibility, the game maintains a high degree of replayability and keeps progression feeling fresh even after many hours. The roguelite-inspired structure further enhances the experience. While players gain knowledge and experience over time, every journey into the Necrovale presents new opportunities and challenges. Adapting to the items found during a run becomes a key part of the gameplay loop. Some of the most memorable moments occur when seemingly average equipment unexpectedly combines into a powerful setup capable of turning a difficult situation into a triumphant victory. The constant potential for discovery keeps the gameplay engaging from start to finish. Visually, the game employs detailed pixel art that complements its dark fantasy themes remarkably well. The environments are filled with decaying ruins, eerie landscapes, and hostile territories that reinforce the sense of exploring a forgotten world. Despite its retro-inspired presentation, the visual design is rich with atmosphere and personality. Enemy designs are varied and distinctive, helping every encounter feel meaningful while contributing to the overall sense of danger. The characters encountered throughout the adventure add another layer of depth. Rather than meeting traditional heroes, players interact with fellow outcasts, prisoners, and damaged individuals who have their own stories and motivations. These encounters help flesh out the setting and create a world that feels populated by people struggling to survive under harsh circumstances. The moral ambiguity surrounding many of these characters makes them more interesting than typical fantasy archetypes. One of the game's greatest achievements is how effectively it rewards curiosity. Exploration often leads to valuable discoveries, whether through hidden treasures, powerful equipment, or new pieces of lore. The game trusts players to experiment and learn through experience rather than relying on excessive tutorials. This design philosophy makes progression feel natural and satisfying, allowing players to develop a genuine sense of mastery over time. Although the game excels in many areas, it may not appeal equally to everyone. Players looking for a heavily narrative-driven experience may find the storytelling somewhat understated. Likewise, those who prefer a more guided structure could occasionally feel overwhelmed by the freedom provided by the item system. However, for players who enjoy discovering mechanics on their own and crafting unique builds, these elements are more likely to be strengths than weaknesses. Into the Necrovale stands out as an impressive blend of action RPG combat, deep loot customization, and atmospheric world-building. Its rich equipment system, rewarding exploration, and emphasis on player experimentation create an experience that remains engaging long after the first few hours. By combining challenging combat with endless build possibilities and a compellingly mysterious setting, the game delivers a memorable adventure that fans of dark fantasy and loot-driven RPGs are likely to find highly rewarding. Rating: 8/10

Into the Necrovale really surprised me. I expected a run of the mill roguelite, but was met with an impressively deep ARPG with roguelike mission structure. The build diversity and possibilities is staggering. I’m usually not one to mess around with build craft, but the systems at play here make every choice meaningful. There is a “meld” system at play here where you can merge two items of the same type together to combine their benefits (or downsides). It can’t be understated how incredible this system is. For weapons, this makes for some insane combos. My two favorite combinations were: 1) Taking a sword that spun around me and melding it with a spear that stunned enemies and electrified them (which made them take more damage). I then used a helmet that stunned enemies in a radius when I stunned a single enemy, an amulet that make me spin more times per attack, and other items to turn me super sayan. So in true spin to win fashion, I was a lawnmower from Hell. 2) I took the sniper-like bow, the Deadeye, which has super high base damage, and melded it with a staff that brought in the “sequence” effect of 10, which means for every attack I made, it would be followed up with 10 additional attacks in rapid sequence. I then used items to “add attacks” which turned the bow into more of a spread fire weapon, gloves that added more damage per sequence, etc. I was covering the screen with high damage heat seeking arrows by the end. This is just two examples of weapons melds. You can meld any slot type (hats, armors, boots, gloves, etc), of which there are 12 total equipment slots. Then, in the endgame, you gain the ability to meld a third item into each combination, which is just insanity and leads to even more possibility. I decided to try melding a bow that shot explosive arrows onto the bow I mentioned above. I was shooting hundreds of arrows a second all with a large explosion on each arrow. My CPU didn’t like that one too much. But my dopamine sure did. If you like ARPGs or have any desire to engage with build craft systems, this game is elite. The combat loop is simple, but it doesn’t get boring as you’re constantly iterating and growing stronger. I’m coming to this game late, so it looks like all the balancing patches and such were already completed. Even with the chaos above, everything still feels fair. Even with broken builds, I’d still get one shot as a glass cannon. The dev also seemed very engaged on threads over the last couple of years which was great to see. Also, played the entire thing on steam deck. Worked amazing aside from when I ran into the situation I mentioned above.

It might be a good game beneath the controller issues. I own two USB controllers and this game has problems with both of them. I have a bad controller with jammed buttons (not the game's fault, I know) that the game simply reads as an XBox controller and gives me XBox prompts, which are a perversion of Nintendo prompts, and thus I have to rotate the controller in my mind when the game tells me to press a button. My good controller with well functioning buttons the game doesn't recognize so I have to use a third party key mapping program. At first this seemed like a double win because I could manipulate the game into calling the buttons what I call them, but this too was problematic. You still have to use the mouse to navigate the inventory, which is annoying, but what makes the game unplayable is the fact that your character only attacks in the direction of the mouse cursor if the game doesn't detect a controller. There's a similar "feature" in Wizard of Legend, but the devs had the good sense to allow you to deactivate it. I've honestly lost count of how many times a game was almost ruined because the devs didn't think through these controller issues, from not letting you edit the configuration, not letting you change the prompts, or not detecting your controller in the first place. This is honestly the first time the problem was completely unsolvable with third party programs running in the background. I've been using emulators for decades and I've never had a single issue with literally any controller I've ever used. I don't know how this is so hard to get right in a game I actually paid money for.
